cards.q: What does '5/2' mean on a pneumatic valve?
options: 5 bar and 2 litres a second
5 ports and 2 positions
5 mm bore and 2 solenoids
Model 5, version 2
cards.why: Ports: supply, two outlets and two exhausts. Positions: the two states the spool can be in.

cards.q: A cylinder with a {d} mm bore runs at {p} bar. What force does it push with, ignoring friction, in newtons?
cards.why: $F = pA$. 1 bar is 0.1 N/mm², and the piston area is $\pi r^2$ in mm².

cards.q: A 5/3 valve with a closed centre is in its middle position. What does the cylinder do?
options: Held roughly where it is: all ports blocked
It extends slowly under the supply
It vents and the piston goes slack
It returns home under spring force
cards.why: Closed centre traps the air on both sides. It holds position only roughly (air compresses, and seals leak); an exhaust (open) centre would let it float.

cards.q: How does a PLC usually know a cylinder has reached the end of its stroke?
options: It times how long the stroke takes
It watches the supply pressure drop
The valve reports it back by itself
A magnetic sensor on the barrel
cards.why: Reed or Hall sensors clip to the cylinder body at each end. Timing alone cannot tell a jam from a finished move.

cards.q: Why are cylinder speeds usually controlled by meter-out (throttling the exhaust)?
options: It uses much less compressed air
It gives more force at the stroke's end
The trapped exhaust cushions the piston
Meter-in is not possible with air
cards.why: Throttling the air leaving the cylinder holds back the piston against a cushion, so it cannot lurch. Meter-in suits single-acting cylinders.

cards.q: A single-solenoid, spring-return 5/2 valve loses its electrical signal. What does the cylinder do?
options: It stops exactly where it is
The spring shifts the valve and it returns home
It carries on to the end it was going to
Nothing, until the air is removed
cards.why: Spring return has one rest state. A double-solenoid valve keeps its last position instead, which is safer or less safe depending on the machine.

cards.q: A hydraulic cylinder has a {d} mm bore and works at {p} bar. What force does it make, in kN?
cards.why: $F = pA$: bar × 0.1 gives N/mm²; × area in mm² gives N; ÷ 1000 for kN.

cards.q: {q} L/min flows into a cylinder with a {d} mm bore. How fast does it extend, in m/s?
cards.why: Speed = flow ÷ area: L/min ÷ 60 000 is m³/s; the area in m².

cards.q: A pump delivers {q} L/min at {p} bar. What hydraulic power is that, in kW?
cards.why: Power = pressure × flow; with bar and L/min, kW = bar × L/min ÷ 600.

cards.q: What does a proportional valve do that an on-off valve does not?
options: It opens in proportion to its signal
It switches over much faster
It works with no electrical power
It holds pressure with no leakage
cards.why: The spool's position follows the command, so speed and force can be controlled smoothly.

cards.q: Why is oil cleanliness so important for servo and proportional valves?
options: Dirty oil turns a darker colour
Clean oil is thinner and flows better
It only matters for the pump itself
Clearances of a few microns jam or wear
cards.why: Filtration to the valve maker's cleanliness class (ISO 4406) is part of the valve's specification.

cards.q: Why does a servo valve need position feedback to put a cylinder in a given place?
options: Servo valves only work with feedback
Feedback cools the valve's coil
The valve sets speed, so position drifts
To measure the oil temperature
cards.why: Opening sets speed, and small leaks and offsets integrate into position error. A closed position loop corrects it continuously.

cards.q: Water flows at {v1} m/s in a {d1} mm pipe, which narrows to {d2} mm. How fast does it flow in the narrow part, in m/s?
cards.why: The same volume passes each second: v × area is constant, and area goes with diameter squared.

cards.q: Water (1000 kg/m³) speeds up from {v1} m/s to {v2} m/s in a level pipe. By Bernoulli, how much does its pressure fall, in kPa?
cards.why: $\Delta p = \frac{1}{2}\rho(v_2^2 - v_1^2)$: faster flow, lower pressure.

cards.q: Water (1000 kg/m³) flows at {v} m/s through {l} m of {d} mm pipe, with friction factor 0.02. What is the pressure loss, in kPa? ($\Delta p = f\frac{L}{D}\frac{1}{2}\rho v^2$)
cards.why: Darcy–Weisbach: losses grow with length and with speed squared, and fall with diameter.

cards.q: A pump gives {q} m³/h at full speed. A VFD runs it at {pc}% speed. What flow do the affinity laws predict, in m³/h?
cards.why: Flow goes with speed.

cards.q: A pump gives a head of {h} m at full speed. What head does it give at {pc}% speed, in m?
cards.why: Head (pressure) goes with speed squared.

cards.q: A fan takes {p} kW at full speed. Slowed by a VFD to {pc}% speed, what power do the affinity laws predict, in kW?
cards.why: Power goes with speed cubed: 80% speed is about half the power. That is why a VFD saves so much over a damper.

cards.q: Match each way heat moves with an example.
pairs: Heat flowing through a heatsink's metal
A fan blowing air over the heatsink fins
Warmth felt from a furnace door, through air
cards.why: Conduction through solids; convection carried by a moving fluid; radiation as infrared, needing nothing in between.

cards.q: Heat conducts through a {x} mm steel plate (k = 50 W/m·K) of {a} m², with {dt} °C across it. How much heat flows, in watts?
cards.why: $Q = \frac{kA\Delta T}{d}$, with the thickness in metres.

cards.q: A surface's absolute temperature (in kelvin) is multiplied by {r}. By what factor does the heat it radiates rise?
cards.why: Stefan–Boltzmann: radiated power goes with absolute temperature to the fourth power.

cards.q: What does the first law of thermodynamics say?
options: Heat flows from cold to hot
Energy is conserved
Nothing can reach absolute zero
All engines are fully efficient
cards.why: Energy is never made or lost, only moved or changed in form. The second law says which way heat flows.

cards.q: A motor delivers {po} kW at {e}% efficiency. How much heat does it give off, in kW?
cards.why: Input = output ÷ efficiency; everything not delivered as work becomes heat.

cards.q: A heat engine runs between {th} °C and {tc} °C. What is the most efficient it could possibly be (Carnot), in %?
cards.why: $\eta_{max} = 1 - \frac{T_c}{T_h}$, with both temperatures in kelvin (°C + 273.15).

cards.q: A {p} kW drive loses about 3% of its rating as heat inside the panel. How many watts is that?
cards.why: 3% of the drive's power, in watts. The drive's manual gives the exact figure.

cards.q: A panel must shed {q} W with the air inside at most {dt} K above outside. Using airflow (m³/h) = 3.1 × watts ÷ ΔT, what fan flow does it need?
cards.why: The 3.1 comes from the density and heat capacity of air near sea level. A smaller allowed rise needs more air.

cards.q: A panel's walls shed 5.5 W per m² per K. It has {a} m² of free surface, {dt} K warmer than outside, and {q} W of losses inside. How many watts are left for a fan or cooler to remove?
cards.why: The walls remove $kA\Delta T$; the rest must go by fan or cooler.
